slides.title: Chapter 3 Job Analysis
slides.subtitle: Human Resource Management · Sample deck
slides.meta: Generated by lecture-ppt-workflow · Original teaching sample
slides.notes: About one minute. Open with a question: a manager asks HR to hire "someone capable". How can HR turn "capable" into something concrete? That leads into job analysis.

items: What job analysis is and why it matters
slides.notes: Walk through the five parts. This deck covers the first of two class sessions.

slides.title: What job analysis is
slides.notes: Transition: first, be clear about what job analysis actually analyzes.

slides.title: Defining job analysis
slides.definition: Systematically collecting information about a job to define its duties, working conditions and the knowledge, skills and abilities it requires.
points: Object: the job itself, not an employee
Role: the foundation of many HR activities
slides.notes: Stress three key ideas: systematic collection, the job, and job requirements. Common misconception: students often think job analysis evaluates how well an employee performs. Make clear that it studies the job, which is different from performance appraisal. Ask students to name two or three duties of a familiar job, such as a teaching assistant.

slides.title: Why job analysis matters
points: Recruitment: clear hiring criteria, not first impressions
Training: compare people with the job to find skill gaps
Performance: clear duties give appraisal a basis
Pay: information for evaluating each job
slides.emphasis: Job analysis is the common starting point for hiring, training, appraisal and pay
slides.notes: For each item, ask what happens without job analysis: vague hiring criteria, untargeted training, disputed appraisals, pay that people do not accept. Transition: so how is job analysis actually done?

slides.title: The job analysis process
slides.notes: Transition: job analysis is a process with clear stages.

slides.title: Four stages

steps.title: Preparation
steps.text: Set the purpose, choose target jobs, form a working group

steps.title: Investigation
steps.text: Choose methods, collect duties, tasks and conditions

steps.title: Analysis
steps.text: Organize and verify information, summarize requirements

steps.title: Completion
steps.text: Write the documents and revise them as they are used

slides.notes: About three minutes, one stage at a time. Point out that the purpose shapes the method: analysis for hiring focuses on job requirements, analysis for pay focuses on the value of the job. Completion is not the end; when the job changes, the documents must be updated. This links to the case later.

slides.title: Common methods
slides.notes: Transition: which methods collect the information in the investigation stage?

slides.title: Comparing four methods
slides.note: In practice, combine several methods so they confirm each other
slides.notes: Compare the four methods across each column, about four minutes. Ask: to analyze an assembly-line worker and a software engineer, which method would you choose first for each? Guide students to see that observation suits the first, while interviews and questionnaires suit the second.

slides.title: Job description and specification
slides.notes: Transition: the results of job analysis are written up in two parts.

slides.title: Two parts of the result

columns.title: Job description: what is the job?
Job specification: who can do it well?

slides.conclusion: The description is about the work; the specification is about the person
slides.notes: Compare the two columns side by side. Common mistake: students put "good communication skills" under duties; explain that it belongs in the specification. Ask students to sort "prepares the monthly report" and "proficient in Excel" into the right column.

slides.title: Why the job description failed
slides.material: A sales team's job descriptions are three years old. A new account manager spends half her time on data analysis and client follow-up, but her description only says "develop the market and meet sales targets". Her supervisor appraises her against it, and they disagree.
questions: What is wrong with this job description?
How should the company improve its job analysis?
analysis: The description no longer matches the work
slides.notes: About five minutes. Let students read the material, then discuss in small groups for two minutes. A likely answer is "the employee should follow the description"; follow up by asking who should update the description when the duties change. Click to reveal the suggested analysis and stress that job analysis needs ongoing maintenance.

slides.title: Check your understanding

questions.q: Does job analysis study the job or the employee?
questions.answer: The job: its duties and requirements, not one person's performance.

questions.q: Is observation enough to analyze an R&D engineer's job?
questions.answer: No. The work is mainly mental; add interviews and questionnaires.

slides.notes: Let students answer each question first, then click to show the answer. For question 2, follow up: which other method could help? (The work diary.)

slides.title: Chapter map
slides.notes: Spend one minute walking along the four branches with the class. Ask students: which kind of job suits each method best?

slides.title: Homework
slides.subtitle: Pick a job you know well and write its job description and job specification (3–5 items each)
slides.notes: Set the homework. Two submissions will be discussed in the next class.
